title: Algebraic = Integral over a Field
content: The four ring-closure lemmas (isAlgebraic_add/neg/sub/mul) share one move: rewrite IsAlgebraic to IsIntegral via isAlgebraic_iff_isIntegral, then apply Mathlib's integral-closure subring lemmas IsIntegral.add/neg/sub/mul. The rewrite is valid precisely because K is a field — over a general ring 'algebraic' and 'integral' diverge. This reuses, rather than re-proves, the deep fact that integral elements form a subring (whose proof goes through finitely generated modules and the determinant trick).
mathContext: Over a field $K$, $x$ is algebraic over $K$ iff $x$ is integral over $K$. The integral elements of any $K$-algebra form a subring, so algebraicity inherits closure under $+, -, \times$.

title: Closure Under Inversion
content: The multiplicative inverse is the one operation integrality alone does not give: 1/2 is integral over Z but its inverse is not, so the subring lemmas stop short. Algebraicity over a field, however, is closed under inversion — isAlgebraic_inv simply invokes Mathlib's IsAlgebraic.inv. Geometrically, if x satisfies a polynomial of degree n, then x⁻¹ satisfies the reversed (palindromic) polynomial, so it too is algebraic.
mathContext: If $\sum_{i=0}^n c_i x^i = 0$ with $c_0 \neq 0$, then $\sum_{i=0}^n c_{n-i} (x^{-1})^i = 0$: the reversed polynomial annihilates $x^{-1}$.

title: algebraicSubfield: Packaging the Closure as a Subfield
content: The six closure lemmas (mul, one, add, zero, neg, inv) are exactly the Subfield axioms, so they assemble into algebraicSubfield K L : Subfield L with carrier {x | IsAlgebraic K x}. Instantiated at K = Q, L = C this is the field of algebraic numbers; combined with the parent's countability result it upgrades 'countable set' to 'countable subfield of C'. The @[simp] membership lemma mem_algebraicSubfield exposes the carrier definitionally.
mathContext: $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} = \{x \in \mathbb{C} : x \text{ algebraic over } \mathbb{Q}\}$ is a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ — and, being countable, a countable algebraically closed field.

title: The Back-Substitution Contradiction
content: Every transcendence-preservation theorem is the contrapositive of a §1 closure lemma, proved by the same one-line trick. To show t + a is transcendental, assume it is algebraic; then t = (t + a) − a is a difference of two algebraic numbers, hence algebraic by isAlgebraic_sub — contradicting transcendence of t. Subtraction, the additive variants, and (with a⁻¹) the multiplicative cases all follow this single template, which is why the proofs are uniformly short.
mathContext: If $t+a$ were algebraic and $a$ is algebraic, then $t = (t+a) - a$ is algebraic — contradicting $t \notin \overline{K}$. The transcendentals form a single orbit-complement under the algebraic affine group.

title: Why Nonzero Is Required for Rescaling
content: For products the back-substitution recovers t as a⁻¹·(a·t), which only makes sense when a ≠ 0 — hence the ha0 : a ≠ 0 hypothesis. The proof multiplies the assumed-algebraic a·t by the algebraic a⁻¹ and simplifies via inv_mul_cancel_left₀. The degenerate case a = 0 genuinely fails: 0·t = 0 is algebraic for every t, so the nonzero hypothesis is not a technicality but a true boundary of the statement.
mathContext: $t = a^{-1}(a t)$ requires $a \neq 0$; indeed $0 \cdot t = 0 \in \overline{K}$, so rescaling by $0$ destroys transcendence.

title: The Affine Map Capstone
content: transcendental_affine packages all the additive and multiplicative cases: for a ≠ 0 and a, b algebraic, the map t ↦ a·t + b sends transcendentals to transcendentals. It is proved by composing transcendental_algebraic_mul (for a·t) with transcendental_add_algebraic (for +b). This is the form used in practice: it says the set of transcendentals is invariant under the entire group of algebraic affine transformations x ↦ a·x + b.
mathContext: The algebraic affine group $\{x \mapsto ax+b : a,b \in \overline{K},\ a \neq 0\}$ acts on $L$ and preserves the transcendentals setwise.

title: The Transcendentals Are Not a Subfield
content: The sharp contrast with §1: for any transcendental t, both t and 1−t are transcendental (the latter by transcendental_algebraic_sub), yet their sum t + (1−t) = 1 is algebraic. So the transcendentals are closed under no field operation. The structural reason is that they are the set-theoretic complement of the algebraic subfield — and the complement of a nontrivial subfield is never itself closed under addition or multiplication.
mathContext: $t + (1-t) = 1 \in \overline{K}$ with $t, 1-t \notin \overline{K}$. A subfield's complement is closed under no field operation.

title: Concrete Witnesses over ℚ ⊆ ℂ
content: The Examples section instantiates the general theorems at K = Q, L = C: for any transcendental t, the numbers t+1, t⁻¹, t², and 1−t are transcendental. Existence of such t is guaranteed abstractly (the transcendentals have cardinality 𝔠, per the sibling leaf) and concretely by classical results: e (Hermite 1873), π (Lindemann 1882), and every Liouville number. From a single such t the affine-orbit toolkit yields infinitely many transcendentals for free.
mathContext: $e, \pi$ transcendental $\Rightarrow e+1,\ e^2,\ 1/e,\ 2\pi-3,\ \ldots$ all transcendental; Liouville's $\sum 10^{-n!}$ is an explicit transcendental.
